abstract: Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation (SDMC) plays a vital role in facilitating the retention of newly learnt information. However, retesting in the literature is scarce and thus little is known regarding the daily stability of the SDMC process. The present study investigated whether overnight memory consolidation performance is stable (reflecting a trait) or variable (reflecting a state) across two nights using a novel word-pair smartphone application. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of subjective sleep quality and motivation on overnight consolidation performance, and whether these associations remained consistent across nights. Young healthy adults (N = 52) completed a validated word-pair task via a smartphone application over two nights and completed subjective sleep and motivation questionnaires. Results indicated overnight consolidation performance was not stable across nights, despite same-day and next-day recall exhibiting significant stability. Subjective sleep and motivation scores were not associated with performance, although these associations remained consistent across nights. However, worse PSQI scores were associated with lower next-day recall. After considering semantically related and unrelated word-pairs, both same-day and next-day recall performance exhibited significant stability for unrelated word-pairs only. These findings question the reliance on single-night SDMC protocols, and future research should examine modifiable factors that underlie SDMC variability across nights.
